patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] btrfs: downgrade the reflink source inode lock

version_history.subject: [PATCH] btrfs: downgrade the reflink source inode lock

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Btrfs file system to downgrade the lock on the source inode during a reflink operation from exclusive to shared, reducing contention and improving performance. The change also adds a flag to indicate when an inode is being used as a reflink source, which allows direct I/O writes to take the VFS inode lock in shared mode instead of exclusive mode. This patch was tested with concurrent readers and writers and showed significant latency improvements.

review_comments.author: Filipe Manana
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that taking the inode's rwsem in shared mode during reflink may not provide significant benefits if only a portion of the file is being reflinked and direct IO reads occur on a different range, requesting clarification in the change log.

Filipe Manana noted that direct IO reads and writes increment the i_dio_count by calling inode_dio_begin(), which may lead to issues, and suggested this as a valid concern
review_comments.raw_body:
You mean a direct IO read operation happening in parallel with a
reflink using the same file as a source right?
And reflinking the entire file?

Because we only take the VFS lock (rwsem in struct inode) for direct IO reads.

However during reads (both direct IO and buffered) we always lock the
extent range in the inode's extent io tree, and the reflink also locks
the range.
So taking the rwsem in shared mode won't help much unless we are not
reflinking the whole file and direct IO reads happen on a different
range.
I think that should be explicit in the change log.

---

There is also an issue pointed out by sashiko that seems valid to me:

https://sashiko.dev/#/patchset/65fa79581e1d29d6d6fabae71d23e741bff0ddf9.1788974902.git.boris%40bur.io

As every direct IO read and write increment i_dio_count with a call to
inode_dio_begin() in iomap.

Thanks.

sentiment_signals: admitted to missing a key detail

I will make the test cases much more explicit in future versions of this
work, if something else comes together that makes sense in light of the

Unfortunately, I think this bug is fully disqualifying for this
exact approach. I didn't notice that (or test it, clearly..)

I started this line of reasoning with pre-flushing the src outside the
lock, then found I wanted to downgrade the lock for the extent writing
after the prep stuff, then had the "insight" that just downgrading would
have the same effect but missed this detail. So I will try again with
the pre-flush + smaller scoped downgrade.

review_comments.summary: Author Boris Burkov responded to feedback from Filipe Manana, acknowledging that the patch's approach may be unnecessary due to a prior change (5d6f0e9890ed) that already avoids locking the source extent range during reflink. He asked if he was missing something else.

we don't lock the src extent range, so dio reads of the src should not

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 0/5] KVM: guest_memfd: bind backing memory to a NUMA node

version_history.subject: [PATCH 0/5] KVM: guest_memfd: bind backing memory to a NUMA node

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/5] mm/mempolicy: add mempolicy_create()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function, mempolicy_create(), which creates and validates a memory policy without installing it into the current task's policy. The function takes mode, flags, and nodes as arguments, allocates a new policy, constrains it to the task's cpuset, and returns the policy or an error pointer on failure. This patch also exports the symbol for use in guest_memfd integration with KVM.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/5] mm/mempolicy: add mpol_set_shared_policy_range()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function mpol_set_shared_policy_range() that allows installing an already-built memory policy over an arbitrary page range without requiring a VMA. The existing mpol_set_shared_policy() function is reimplemented as a thin wrapper to derive the range from the VMA, allowing both functions to share a single underlying path. This change addresses limitations in the current implementation that make it unusable for binding entire backing inodes from in-kernel code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/5] KVM: guest_memfd: bind backing memory to a NUMA node at creation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new flag called GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE to the KVM guest memory file descriptor (memfd) feature. When this flag is set, the backing memory for the guest is bound to a specific NUMA node at creation time, rather than being allocated through a shared mempolicy that can be modified later. This change requires CONFIG_NUMA to be enabled and only allows binding to nodes within the calling task's cpuset. The policy is fixed for the life of the fd and cannot be rebound on later cpuset changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/5] selftests: KVM: guest_memfd: let the gmem_test() harness bind a node
series_items.patch_summary: This patch extends the create_guest_memfd() function to accept a node argument, allowing the gmem_test() harness to bind a node when creating a guest memory file descriptor. The BIND_NODE flag is used to determine whether the node argument should be ignored or used for binding. This change enables testing of GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE functionality.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/5] selftests: KVM: guest_memfd: test GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds tests for the GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE flag in KVM's guest_memfd feature. The tests cover various scenarios, including single and multi-node systems, invalid arguments, and edge cases such as non-zero padding and out-of-range node numbers. The tests ensure that the BIND_NODE flag behaves correctly when used with other flags and when faults occur on remote nodes.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series adds a new flag to the KVM guest memory file descriptor (memfd) API, allowing users to bind the backing memory of the guest to a specific NUMA node. This is done by creating an MPOL_BIND policy for the requested node and installing it over the whole inode, ensuring that every folio is allocated on the specified node without requiring user-space mbind(). The patch series also includes self-test harness support and testing to validate the new functionality. The approach taken is to simplify the guest NUMA topology by binding a single fd to a host node, rather than interleaving it across multiple nodes, which would defeat placement decisions made by the guest.

review_comments.author: Ackerley Tng
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Ackerley Tng suggested alternative approaches to ensure guest_memfd allocations come from a single node, including using cgroups/cpuset, process-level NUMA policy, requesting mmap-ability for memory policy setting, fbind() API, or passing an fd representing a mount with a specified memory policy.
review_comments.raw_body:
Instead of a custom API to ensure all guest_memfd allocations come from
a single node, how about these options?

1. Using cgroups/cpuset to constrain allocations (could be troublesome
   if the guest memory is not preallocated, unless the vCPU threads are
   running with the cpuset config)

2. Process-level NUMA policy

3. Why not request the guest_memfd to be mmap-able just to be able to
   set a memory policy?

4. How about something like fbind() that takes an fd and offset range
   instead of mbind(), which has a prerequisite on mmap()?

This doesn't exist yet, but I'm hoping to discuss this at LPC 2026:

5. What if you could pass an fd representing a mount to guest_memfd at
   creation time, so to make all the allocations come from a single node

    Step 1: Create a tmpfs mount, specify mpol for mount to MPOL_BIND
    Step 2: Get some fd representing the tmpfs mount, hand that to
            guest_memfd at creation time
    Step 3: guest_memfd allocations will always come from that tmpfs
            mount, and abide by that tmpfs mount's memory policy.

May I know more about the use case behind this new feature?

review_comments.author: Gregory Price (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author clarified that the intent of GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE is to bind guest memory to a specific target node, not all system memory for a given process, and acknowledged that the desired node may not have eligible memory.

Author acknowledged that requiring a mapping to set node placement defeats the purpose of confidential, host-unmapped guests and plans to enable this for such use cases.

The author is addressing concerns about the scope and implementation of guest_memfd, specifically where the policy lives for random file descriptors (fd's) and how a reclaimed inode's policy is handled. The author acknowledges these limitations but prefers to start with a narrow use-case, considering it less over-engineering than implementing per-file mempolicies.

Author acknowledges that implementing a single-node binding approach is more feasible than using fbind, but expresses uncertainty about the complexity of details.

Author acknowledged that the patch's approach of binding guest memory to a single node is necessary for modeling a confidential VM's topology and explained that this implementation enables the only clear use case.

Reviewer Ackerley Tng suggested that the policy would be saved at gi->policy, which is where it's currently stored for mbind(), and noted that fd+offset is just another way of referencing offsets to set the policy.

Reviewer Ackerley Tng noted that the patch does not address HugeTLBfs and suggested adding a similar mechanism for configuring HugeTLB page size, but also mentioned that it would not help with memcg since tmpfs does not offer a way to configure them.

Reviewer Ackerley Tng questioned whether lazy allocation is necessary, suggesting that pre-allocating memory using fallocate() before the guest accesses pages might be sufficient.

review_comments.raw_body:

charged a certain memcg. Currently guest_memfd memory is charge to
mm->owner, which is the thread's parent, so doing the fallocate() in a
thread wasn't good enough. The workaround was to have the fallocate()
done in a separate process (fork) and have the child process's memcg be
set to the desired memcg.

This workaround is kind of awkward, but could it technically work for
NUMA allocations?

Off the top of my head the policy would be saved at gi->policy, where

referencing the offsets to set the policy.

review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that since only the VMA is needed for setting the policy, it can be dropped after installation, and suggested removing it to improve performance.

Reviewer David expressed concerns that the patch's approach to binding backing memory to a NUMA node may not be suitable for private-only guest_memfd, as it relies on consuming pages from the guest_memfd regardless of whether they are shared or private. review_comments.author: Gregory Price (author)
review_comments.summary: The author clarifies the relationship between the guest_memfd inode's mempolicy and the task's mempolicy, explaining that it acts as a filesystem-default policy that survives even if userland unmmaps the memory. They also outline an example use case for setting KVM_MEMORY_ATTRIBUTE_PRIVATE to limit guest access to specific memory ranges.
review_comments.raw_body:
Ah yes, i do remember this series.  In fact...

https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/aPD-dbl5KWNSHu5R@gourry-fedora-PF4VCD3F/

```
So this inode mempolicy in guest_memfd is really acting more as a the
filesystem-default mempolicy, which you want to survive even if userland
never maps the memory/unmaps the memory.

So the relationship is more like

guest_memfd -> creates fd/inode <- copies task mempolicy (if set)
  vm:  allocates memory via filemap_get_folio_mpol()
  userland mmap(fd):
  	creates new inode<->vma mapping
	vma->mpol = kvm_gmem_get_policy()
	calls to set/get_policy/mbind go through kvm_gmem
```

And quick skim of in-place conversion (wow that's dense) 

```
  #define KVM_MEMORY_ATTRIBUTE_PRIVATE           (1ULL << 3)

  Set attributes for a range of offsets within a guest_memfd to
  KVM_MEMORY_ATTRIBUTE_PRIVATE to limit the specified guest_memfd backed
  memory range for guest use. Even if KVM_CAP_GUEST_MEMFD_MMAP is
  supported, after a successful call to set KVM_MEMORY_ATTRIBUTE_PRIVATE,
  the requested range will not be mappable into host userspace and will
  only be mappable by the guest.
```

I guess the thought here would be something like...

1. create guest memfd
2. mmap(fd)               -> prior to full guest setup
3. mbind(buf)             -> shared policy hits the inode
4. munmap(buf)            -> policy is NOT reaped
5. set ATTRIBUTE_PRIVATE
6. no longer user mappable

That doesn't seem unreasonable

~Gregory

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 0/7] nfsdctl: allow it to handle rpcbind registration and deregistration

version_history.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 0/7] nfsdctl: allow it to handle rpcbind registration and deregistration

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 1/7] nfsdctl: sync nfsd_netlink.h with the kernel
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the nfsd_netlink.h file in the nfs-utils package to match the latest version from the kernel. It imports new attributes related to rpcbind registration, including NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_USERSPACE_RPCBIND and NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_RPCBIND. The patch also adds a test for these new attributes and bumps the USE_SYSTEM_NFSD_NETLINK_H probe to one of the new attributes. This change is necessary because some hosts may have headers that are newer than v6.9, which introduced NFSD_CMD_SERVER_STATS_GET.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 2/7] nfsdctl: probe the policy of any command
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the nfsdctl utility to probe the policy of any command, not just THREADS_SET. It introduces a new function query_nfsd_nl_cmd_policy() that takes the command number as an argument and writes the highest attribute through its callback argument. The original query_nfsd_nl_policy() function is preserved for backwards compatibility and still probes THREADS_SET. No functional changes are made, but the code is refactored to make it more flexible and reusable.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 3/7] nfsdctl: share the listener nest parser
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the listener nest parser in nfsdctl to improve code organization and efficiency. The existing parse_listener_get function is split into two functions: parse_sock_nest, which unpacks a NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_ADDR nest, and the original parse_listener_get function, which now only iterates over top-level attributes. This change allows for better handling of mixed attribute replies and prevents counting non-listener attributes as listeners. The patch makes no functional changes to the code's behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 4/7] nfsdctl: add rpcbind registration helpers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds rpcbind registration helpers to the nfsdctl utility, allowing it to register and unregister NFS services with the local rpcbind. The code ensures that only valid registrations are made, based on rules defined by the kernel's behavior. The patch also moves the struct server_socket definition to a new header file and updates the Makefile to include the new files.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 5/7] nfsdctl: register nfsd listeners with rpcbind
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the nfsdctl utility to register NFS and NFSACL listeners with the local rpcbind instead of the kernel. This change addresses a problem where a slow rpcbind could block other NFSD netlink commands due to synchronous calls made by the kernel while holding an internal mutex. The new approach involves sending a flag, reading the reply, and then registering the listeners without holding any locks. The patch also includes support for detecting whether the kernel supports this feature and handles cases where registration fails or is not supported.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 6/7] nfsdctl: clear rpcbind entries when the last thread stops
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the nfsdctl command to clear rpcbind entries when the last thread stops. The previous behavior was incorrect, as it relied on a kernel function that is no longer used. The patch fixes this issue by checking if all threads have stopped and clearing the rpcbind entries only then. This ensures that the rpcbind entries do not outlive the server and point to an unused port.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 7/7] nfsdctl: add missing break in update_listeners()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the nfsdctl utility by adding missing break statements to the update_listeners() function. The bug caused v4 listeners that matched on port and address to be re-tested as sockaddr_in6, leading to incorrect behavior. The patch ensures that each case in the switch statement is properly terminated, preventing fallthrough into subsequent cases.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patchset allows the nfsdctl tool to handle rpcbind registration and deregistration, rather than relying on the kernel to do so. This is achieved by adding support for a new kernel option that tells it not to register with rpcbind, and instead calls out to rpcbind using libtirpc client interfaces from userland. The patchset includes changes to nfsdctl to handle this new behavior, including registering listeners with rpcbind and clearing entries when the last thread stops.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/5] SUNRPC: allow a service to opt out of rpcbind registration
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows a service to opt out of rpcbind registration by introducing a new flag, sv_no_rpcbind, in the svc_serv structure. When this flag is set, the service will not be registered with rpcbind and the code that handles rpcbind registration will skip over it. This change does not affect any existing behavior as no caller has yet set the flag. The patch modifies three files: include/linux/sunrpc/svc.h, net/sunrpc/svc.c, and net/sunrpc/svc_xprt.c.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/5] NFSD: add a userspace-rpcbind flag to listener_set
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series adds a new flag to the listener_set operation in NFSD, allowing userspace to take over rpcbind registration. The kernel will echo this flag in the reply and list the programs and versions that the caller should register for each listener. This change is necessary because lockd still registers itself with rpcbind, even though it owns its own svc_serv.

review_comments.author: Chuck Lever
review_comments.summary: Identified an issue with the wording of the documentation, suggesting that it should accurately describe what listeners are omitted from the reply. Also pointed out a potential regression in the handling of RDMA transport.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, 10 Sep 2026, Jeff Layton wrote:
> Describe the interface that lets a caller take over rpcbind registration.

> --- a/Documentation/netlink/specs/nfsd.yaml
> +++ b/Documentation/netlink/specs/nfsd.yaml
> @@ -483,13 +527,22 @@ operations:
>      -
>        name: listener-set
> -      doc: set nfs running sockets
> +      doc: >-
> +        set nfs running sockets. A request that carries userspace-rpcbind
> +        is answered with a reply rather than a bare ack, and the addr list
> +        in that reply names only the listeners that have an rpcbind netid.

"listeners that have an rpcbind netid" overstates the set. RDMA
listeners have netids (rdma, rdma6) but are omitted from the
reply.

Following the way Solaris handles RDMA transport, NFSD never
registered RDMA itself, so that is not a regression, but the doc
should say what your filter actually selects.


>        attribute-set: server-sock
>        flags: [admin-perm]
>        do:
>          request:
>            attributes:
>              - addr
> +            - userspace-rpcbind
> +        reply:
> +          attributes:
> +            - addr
> +            - userspace-rpcbind
> +            - rpcbind

The spec declares an unconditional reply, but patch 4 sends one only
when the request carried userspace-rpcbind. ynl has no way to express
a conditional reply, and no other in-tree spec does this.

Either always send the reply (drop the userspace_rpcbind gate in
patch 4, so a plain caller simply ignores it), or leave listener-set
without a reply and put the registration data in a separate get
operation. I lean toward always replying; that's is a little more
"declarative".


-- 
Chuck Lever (Come to NFS bake-a-thon! https://nfsv4bat.org)

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/5] NFSD: honour the userspace-rpcbind flag in listener_set
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the handling of rpcbind in the NFSD listener_set function. The first patch, specifically, introduces a flag called userspace-rpcbind that indicates whether the rpcbind call should be made by the kernel or the user space. When this flag is set, the kernel will not make any rpcbind calls, thus avoiding synchronous rpcbind RPCs under nfsd_mutex.

review_comments.author: Chuck Lever
review_comments.summary: Identified a potential issue where the ownership check in the netlink path is not enforced consistently. Suggested moving the mismatch test into nfsd_create_serv() to ensure both paths agree.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, 10 Sep 2026, Jeff Layton wrote:

> --- a/fs/nfsd/nfsctl.c
> +++ b/fs/nfsd/nfsctl.c
> @@ -2111,15 +2112,25 @@ int nfsd_nl_listener_set_doit(struct sk_buff *skb, struct genl_info *info)
> +	userspace_rpcbind = nla_get_flag(info->attrs[NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_USERSPACE_RPCBIND]);
> +
>  	mutex_lock(&nfsd_mutex);
>  
> -	err = nfsd_create_serv(net);
> +	nn = net_generic(net, nfsd_net_id);
> +
> +	if (nn->nfsd_serv && nn->nfsd_serv->sv_no_rpcbind != userspace_rpcbind) {
> +		NL_SET_ERR_MSG(info->extack,
> +			       "cannot change rpcbind ownership while a server exists");
> +		mutex_unlock(&nfsd_mutex);
> +		return -EBUSY;
> +	}
> +
> +	err = nfsd_create_serv(net, userspace_rpcbind);

This ownership check lives only in the netlink path, so it is
enforced in one direction. Consider: the serv is created here with
userspace-rpcbind, then an old rpc.nfsd writes a socket fd to
/proc/fs/nfsd/portlist. __write_ports_addfd() calls
nfsd_create_serv(net, false), which returns 0 at the existing
"if (nn->nfsd_serv) return 0;" without looking at the flag.
svc_addsock() then goes through svc_setup_socket() with pmap_register
set, and svc_register() returns 0 early because sv_no_rpcbind is set.
The write succeeds, and the new listener is neither registered by the
kernel nor reported to the userspace owner. The reverse order gets
-EBUSY from the check above.

Moving the mismatch test into nfsd_create_serv(), where every creator
already funnels, would make both paths agree. The extack message would
need a different home, but the errno is the important part.


-- 
Chuck Lever (Come to NFS bake-a-thon! https://nfsv4bat.org)

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/5] NFSD: report registerable programs in the listener_set reply
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NFSD listener_set reply to include a list of registerable programs and versions that would be registered by nfsd, as well as listeners to register them. This information is only sent when the request asked for it, ensuring older callers still receive a bare acknowledgement. The changes involve adding new functions to calculate the message size and create the message, and modifying existing code to handle the new requirements.

review_comments.author: Chuck Lever
review_comments.summary:
The reviewer noted that after a partial failure in creating listeners, nfsd continues to serve on the first port created and does not send a reply to the caller, which was never informed about the programs to register or the listeners that came up. The reviewer suggested either tearing down the listeners when any of them fails or sending the reply whenever at least one listener exists.

Reviewer Chuck Lever pointed out that genlmsg_new() already includes GENL_HDRLEN in its size calculation, and suggested passing only the attribute payload to avoid double-counting.

The reviewer suggested extracting a helper function that emits one address nest for an xprt to avoid code duplication between nfsd_nl_listener_set_msg() and nfsd_nl_listener_get_doit(), and also noted that the XPT_RPCB_UNREG filter in nfsd_nl_listener_set_msg() only selects TCP and UDP, which should be reflected in the specification.

The reviewer noted that the ACL block in nfsd_support_acl_version() is redundant and can be removed, as it only handles a specific special case for the ACL program version.
review_comments.raw_body:
The second sentence of the comment is not true after a partial
failure. Take a request with userspace-rpcbind carrying {tcp:2049,
tcp:<port already in use>}. The creation loop continues past the
second failure and keeps only the last errno. The 2049 xprt is on
sv_permsocks, so the serv survives the list_empty() check below, but
this gate skips the reply and the caller sees -EADDRINUSE. nfsd is
now serving on 2049 with nothing registered in rpcbind, and the caller
was never told which listeners came up or which programs to register.
The same end state results when nfsd_nl_listener_set_msg() itself
fails with -ENOMEM.

In kernel-owned mode the survivor would already have been registered
inside svc_xprt_create_from_sa(), so this is a behavioral gap specific
to the new mode. Either tear down the listeners that were created when
any of them fails, or send the reply whenever at least one listener
exists on the serv, regardless of err. The second keeps the existing
partial-success semantics; the caller can then act on what it got.

---

genlmsg_new() already adds GENL_HDRLEN via genlmsg_total_size(), so
this term double-counts it. Harmless, but the comment will mislead the
next person sizing a reply. Pass only the attribute payload here.

---

This is the same nest emission as the loop in
nfsd_nl_listener_get_doit(), apart from the XPT_RPCB_UNREG filter and
the errno (that one returns -EINVAL). A small helper that emits one
addr nest for an xprt, called from both loops, would keep the two from
drifting, with the size accounting above as the third place to keep
in step.

Also, as noted on patch 2, this filter selects TCP and UDP only; the
spec doc should match.

---

The ACL block is redundant with the first test. The ACL program has
pg_nvers = NFSD_ACL_NRVERS and pg_vers = nfsd_acl_version, whose
slots 0 and 1 and any compiled-out version are NULL, and
nfsd_support_acl_version() checks exactly that range and that array.
Dropping the block removes the function's only program-number special
case and the #if with it.


-- 
Chuck Lever (Come to NFS bake-a-thon! https://nfsv4bat.org)

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/5] selftests/nfsd: exercise the userspace-rpcbind listener_set flag
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a series of tests to the selftests/nfsd suite to exercise various features and edge cases related to the userspace-rpcbind listener_set flag. The tests cover scenarios such as skipping rpcbind registration, handling NFSv4 and NFSv3 protocols, ownership rules, and error conditions. The patch also updates the genl_request_reply function to handle attribute arguments in the reply message. Overall, this patch aims to ensure that the userspace-rpcbind listener_set flag is properly handled by the kernel and that the selftests/nfsd suite can cover a wide range of scenarios related to NFS services.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series allows userland to handle rpcbind registration for nfsd listeners, providing a new optional flag in the netlink listener set interface that tells the kernel to skip rpcbind registration. This is done by adding a new userspace-rpcbind flag to the listener_set function and honouring it in the listener_set reply. The patch also includes changes to report registerable programs in the listener_set reply and exercises the userspace-rpcbind listener_set flag with selftests. The goal is to allow userland to handle rpcbind registration, while still keeping kernel handling of NLM registration intact.

patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch adds management helpers for NFS to the common/nfs directory, allowing for more efficient and isolated management of NFS services.

review_comments.author: Carlos Maiolino
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Carlos Maiolino expressed concern about the patch's portability to non-systemd init systems, noting that it would be easier to put the test in xfstests if systemd services are used, but acknowledged that this wouldn't be a problem for him personally as he frequently runs xfstests on systemd-based distros.
sentiment_signals: acknowledged it's not a problem for himself
review_comments.raw_body:
My only concern regarding using systemd services is portability. I tried
to keep the test agnostic to the init system being used, but it indeed
would be way easier to put this into xfstests if we just accept this
will be a __not_run on systemd-less distros. Giving the majority of
people I know frequently running xfstests (including me) uses
systemd-based distros, this wouldn't be a problem for me personally...

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledged that using systemd services is a viable solution and would be less likely to bitrot, but expressed concerns about non-systemd cases potentially being neglected.

Author acknowledged Carlos Maiolino's suggestion to consider using systemd services instead of custom scripts, and provided an alternative tool (nfsdctl) for managing the server.
review_comments.raw_body:
That's what I'd probably do. If someone wants to step up and do
something for non-systemd distros then they can have at it.

Alternately, you could use systemd and just fall back to what you're
doing now in the case where it's not present. My only fear there is
that the non-systemd cases would probably bitrot because no one would
use them.

That said, if you're doing all of this in a container then it shouldn't
matter much how it gets started.

---

If you do decide to go this route, note that rpc.nfsd is being
deprecated. We have a new tool for managing the server now called
"nfsdctl" that you probably want to use when possible.
